easy.text: Newton's third law states that for every action, there is:

options.text: An equal and opposite reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- forces always come in equal, opposite pairs.

options.text: A smaller, delayed reaction
options.feedback: The reaction force is equal in size, not smaller, and happens simultaneously, not delayed.

options.text: No reaction at all
options.feedback: The third law specifically states that a reaction force always exists.

options.text: A reaction in the same direction
options.feedback: The reaction force points in the opposite direction, not the same one.

medium.text: When a swimmer pushes backward against the water, what pushes the swimmer forward?

options.text: The water pushing forward on the swimmer with an equal, opposite force
options.feedback: Correct -- this is a direct example of Newton's third law in action.

options.text: The swimmer's own muscles alone, without any outside force
options.feedback: Muscles apply the initial push, but it's the water's reaction force that actually propels the swimmer.

options.text: Gravity pulling the swimmer forward
options.feedback: Gravity pulls straight down, not horizontally forward through water.

options.text: Friction between the swimmer and the pool floor
options.feedback: Swimmers are usually not touching the pool floor while swimming, so this isn't the relevant force.

hard.text: A rocket expels exhaust gas downward at high speed. According to Newton's third law, why does the rocket move upward?

options.text: The gas pushes down on the rocket's surroundings, and an equal, opposite force pushes the rocket up
options.feedback: Correct -- the rocket exerts force on the expelled gas, and the gas exerts an equal, opposite force back on the rocket.

options.text: The rocket is being pulled up by low air pressure above it
options.feedback: Rockets work even in the vacuum of space with no air at all, so air pressure isn't the explanation.

options.text: The exhaust gas becomes lighter than air and rises, carrying the rocket with it
options.feedback: This describes buoyancy, which isn't how rocket propulsion works, especially in space.

options.text: Gravity from the exhaust cloud pulls the rocket upward
options.feedback: Gravitational attraction from exhaust gas would be far too weak to explain rocket motion.

easy.hard: Whatever force one object applies, a matching force in the opposite direction comes right back at it.
easy.medium: Whatever force you apply to something, that thing applies the same force right back at you.
easy.easy: Every push has an equal push back in the opposite direction.

medium.hard: The swimmer applies a backward force on the water, and by the third law, the water applies an equal forward force back on the swimmer.
medium.medium: Whatever force the swimmer applies to the water comes right back at them in the opposite direction.
medium.easy: The water pushes back on the swimmer just as hard as the swimmer pushed on the water.

hard.hard: The rocket exerts a force on the exhaust gas to push it out; by the third law, the gas exerts an equal and opposite force back on the rocket, propelling it forward, with no need for air.
hard.medium: The rocket pushes the gas one way, and the gas pushes the rocket the opposite way with equal force -- no air is needed for this to work.
hard.easy: The rocket pushes gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up just as hard -- this works even with no air around.

easy.text: In a series circuit, how are components connected?

options.text: Along a single path, one after another
options.feedback: Correct -- series circuits have only one path for current to flow through all components in sequence.

options.text: Along multiple separate paths
options.feedback: Multiple separate paths describes a parallel circuit, not a series circuit.

options.text: Not connected at all
options.feedback: A circuit requires connected components to allow current to flow.

options.text: Randomly, with no defined path
options.feedback: Circuits follow defined paths, not random arrangements.

medium.text: What happens to the other bulbs in a series circuit if one bulb burns out?

options.text: All the other bulbs go out too, since the single path is broken
options.feedback: Correct -- a break anywhere in a series circuit's single path stops current everywhere.

options.text: Only the burned-out bulb is affected, the rest stay lit
options.feedback: In a series circuit, there's only one path -- breaking it stops the whole circuit.

options.text: The other bulbs get brighter
options.feedback: With the circuit broken, no current flows at all, so no bulbs would get brighter.

options.text: The circuit automatically switches to parallel
options.feedback: A circuit's basic wiring layout doesn't change on its own during operation.

hard.text: Why do household electrical outlets typically use parallel circuits rather than series circuits?

options.text: So each appliance can operate independently, and one device failing doesn't shut off the others
options.feedback: Correct -- parallel wiring gives each device its own path, so they work independently of each other.

options.text: Because parallel circuits use less wire overall
options.feedback: Parallel circuits typically use more wire, not less, since each path needs its own connection.

options.text: Because parallel circuits can't carry electricity as well
options.feedback: Parallel circuits carry electricity effectively -- that's part of why they're the practical choice.

options.text: Because series circuits are illegal in most buildings
options.feedback: This isn't the reason -- it's a practical/functional choice, not a legal restriction.

easy.hard: There is only one continuous route for current to travel through every component in turn.
easy.medium: Every component sits on the same single loop, one after the other.
easy.easy: All the parts are connected in one single line, one after another.

medium.hard: Since there's only one path in this type of circuit, any break anywhere interrupts current for every component on that path.
medium.medium: Since there's only one path for current, breaking it anywhere stops the flow everywhere on that path.
medium.easy: Since there's only one path, breaking it anywhere stops everything on that path.

hard.hard: Multiple independent paths mean current can keep flowing through unaffected branches even if one branch's device fails or is switched off.
hard.medium: Each appliance gets its own separate path, so one device turning off or breaking doesn't affect the others.
hard.easy: Each device gets its own separate path, so one going out doesn't turn off the rest.

easy.text: What determines the pitch of a sound?

options.text: The frequency of the sound wave
options.feedback: Correct -- higher frequency sound waves are perceived as higher pitch.

options.text: The color of the object making the sound
options.feedback: Color is a visual property, unrelated to how sound pitch is perceived.

options.text: The temperature of the room
options.feedback: Room temperature can slightly affect sound speed, but pitch itself is determined by frequency.

options.text: The weight of the sound wave
options.feedback: Sound waves don't have a 'weight' in this sense -- pitch depends on frequency.

medium.text: A guitar string is tightened, increasing its vibration frequency. What happens to the pitch?

options.text: The pitch gets higher
options.feedback: Correct -- increased frequency directly corresponds to higher pitch.

options.text: The pitch gets lower
options.feedback: Lower pitch would correspond to decreased frequency, the opposite of what's happening here.

options.text: The pitch stays exactly the same
options.feedback: Pitch is directly tied to frequency, so a frequency change must change the pitch.

options.text: The volume increases, but pitch is unaffected
options.feedback: Frequency changes affect pitch specifically, not volume (which relates to amplitude).

hard.text: Two identical guitar strings are stretched to different tensions and plucked. The tighter string produces a higher-pitched sound. What does this tell you about the relationship between tension and frequency?

options.text: Higher tension increases the vibration frequency of the string
options.feedback: Correct -- more tension makes the string vibrate faster, raising both frequency and pitch.

options.text: Higher tension decreases the vibration frequency of the string
options.feedback: This is the opposite -- higher pitch here indicates higher, not lower, frequency.

options.text: Tension has no relationship with frequency at all
options.feedback: The pitch difference observed directly demonstrates that tension does affect frequency.

options.text: Tension only affects volume, not pitch
options.feedback: The scenario describes a pitch change, which is tied to frequency, not simply volume.

easy.hard: This property is measured in how many wave cycles occur each second.
easy.medium: This is how many times the sound wave repeats each second.
easy.easy: How high or low a sound seems depends on how fast the wave vibrates.

medium.hard: A rise in vibration rate translates directly into a rise in how the sound is perceived.
medium.medium: Faster vibration means a higher-sounding pitch.
medium.easy: A faster vibration makes the pitch sound higher, not lower.

hard.hard: Since pitch directly reflects frequency, and the tighter string sounds higher-pitched, tension must be increasing the string's vibration rate.
hard.medium: A higher pitch directly means a higher vibration frequency, so more tension must be raising the frequency.
hard.easy: Since higher pitch means higher frequency, more tension must be making the string vibrate faster.

options.text: Light bouncing off a surface
options.feedback: Correct -- reflection occurs when light bounces back off a surface, like a mirror.

options.text: Light bending as it passes into a new material
options.feedback: That describes refraction, not reflection.

options.text: Light being completely absorbed by a surface
options.feedback: Absorption means the light doesn't bounce back at all, the opposite of reflection.

options.text: Light disappearing entirely
options.feedback: Light energy doesn't just vanish -- it's reflected, absorbed, or transmitted.

medium.text: Why does a straw appear bent when placed in a glass of water?

options.text: Light refracts (bends) as it passes from water into air
options.feedback: Correct -- light changes speed and direction when moving between water and air, creating the bent appearance.

options.text: The straw physically bends when it touches water
options.feedback: The straw itself doesn't actually bend -- it's an optical effect from light bending.

options.text: Light reflects entirely off the surface of the water
options.feedback: Reflection alone wouldn't create the appearance of a bent straw below the surface -- refraction does.

options.text: The water's color distorts the straw's image
options.feedback: Water's clarity or color isn't what causes this bending effect -- it's the change in light's speed and direction.

hard.text: Light travels from air into glass and bends toward the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface). What does this indicate about the light's speed in glass?

options.text: The light slows down in glass
options.feedback: Correct -- bending toward the normal occurs when light slows down entering a denser medium like glass.

options.text: The light speeds up in glass
options.feedback: Speeding up would bend the light away from the normal, not toward it.

options.text: The light's speed is unaffected by entering glass
options.feedback: If speed were unaffected, the light wouldn't bend at all -- refraction only occurs due to a speed change.

options.text: The light stops moving entirely inside the glass
options.feedback: The light continues traveling through the glass, just at a reduced speed, not stopped entirely.

easy.hard: This phenomenon involves light staying in the same medium and bouncing back rather than passing through.
easy.medium: This is what happens when light hits a mirror and comes back toward you.
easy.easy: This is when light bounces off something, like a mirror.

medium.hard: Light travels at different speeds in air versus water, and this speed change bends its path at the boundary.
medium.medium: Light bends when it moves from one material into a different one, like from water to air.
medium.easy: Light changes direction slightly as it moves from water into the air, making the straw look bent.

hard.hard: Bending toward the normal is the signature of light entering an optically denser medium, where its speed decreases.
hard.medium: When light bends toward the normal line, it means the light has slowed down in the new material.
hard.easy: Bending toward that imaginary straight line means the light has slowed down.

easy.text: What happens when two magnets are placed with their like poles (e.g., north to north) facing each other?

options.text: They repel each other
options.feedback: Correct -- like poles repel, while opposite poles attract.

options.text: They attract each other
options.feedback: Attraction happens between opposite poles, not like poles.

options.text: Nothing happens at all
options.feedback: Magnets always exert some force on each other when close, whether repelling or attracting.

options.text: They both lose their magnetism
options.feedback: Simply bringing magnets near each other doesn't erase their magnetism.

medium.text: Which of the following materials is most strongly attracted to a magnet?

options.text: Iron
options.feedback: Correct -- iron is one of the most magnetically attractive common metals.

options.text: Wood
options.feedback: Wood is not magnetic and isn't attracted to magnets.

options.text: Plastic
options.feedback: Plastic is not magnetic and isn't attracted to magnets.

options.text: Glass
options.feedback: Glass is not magnetic and isn't attracted to magnets.

hard.text: A wire carrying an electric current creates a magnetic field around it. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Electricity and magnetism are closely linked phenomena
options.feedback: Correct -- moving electric charge generates a magnetic field, showing the deep connection between electricity and magnetism (electromagnetism).

options.text: All wires are naturally magnetic even without current
options.feedback: A plain wire with no current flowing doesn't produce this magnetic field -- current is required.

options.text: Magnetism can only exist near permanent magnets
options.feedback: This example specifically shows magnetism arising from electric current, not from a permanent magnet.

options.text: The wire must be made of a magnetic metal like iron to show this effect
options.feedback: This effect occurs in ordinary conductive wires (like copper) simply due to current flow, not because the wire itself is magnetic.

easy.hard: Identical poles push away from each other rather than pulling together.
easy.medium: Matching poles push each other away, they don't pull together.
easy.easy: Same poles push apart from each other.

medium.hard: This metal is commonly used in magnetic applications and is a key ingredient in many everyday magnets.
medium.medium: This metal is one of the most common materials that magnets stick to.
medium.easy: This is the metal that fridge magnets often stick to.

hard.hard: This phenomenon is the basis of electromagnetism, showing that a moving electric charge inherently produces a magnetic effect, independent of the wire's material.
hard.medium: This shows that moving electric current itself creates magnetism, not that the wire material is inherently magnetic.
hard.easy: This shows that electricity moving through a wire can create magnetism all on its own.
